title: Pesce All'Acqua Pazza (Southern Italian Poached Fish)
description:
In the early 1800s salt was scarce, even along Italy’s southern coast. So hungry fishermen came up with a “crazy”—and frugal—idea: stewing their catch in seawater. That’s just one story behind pesce all’acqua pazza (“fish in crazy water”), which, over time, evolved considerably into a dish featuring firm‑fleshed white fish cooked in a tomato-studded, garlic-infused broth.
The original recipe calls for skin-on fillets of haddock (or branzino or red snapper), but I also like skinless, meaty halibut. If you don’t have the skin, which adds flavor and richness, you could use a little flour dusting on the sauté and add some butter.
ingredients: 1+/- pound skin-on haddock fillets, or halibut
1+ good dash of red pepper flakes
1 small onion or good-sized shallot, finely chopped
4 ounces (or more) cherry or grape tomatoes, halved
2 handfuls of cooked angel-hair pasta or cooked, leftover rice
directions: Sprinkle fish all over with salt & pepper and set aside.
Heat oil, onion, and pepper flakes in a medium-sized skillet over medium heat, for 2-3 minutes, until onion starts to soften.

Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds. Then add the bay leaf and tomatoes and cook for 2-3 minutes, stirring often. (Here you could sprinkle the mixture with a little flour and add a slice or two of butter.)

Stir in the water, wine, and most of the parsley. Bring to soft boil. Then nestle the fish in, skin-side down, and spoon some of the liquids over the top. Turn the heat down, cover the pan, and simmer gently for 5 minutes or so, until the fish is opaque and just cooked through. Add the pasta or rice and let it come up to temperature for a minute or so.

Season broth with salt & pepper (& pepper flakes) to taste. Put the pasta or rice in the bottom of the serving bowls, carefully add the fish on top, then spoon the other solids and broth over everything, adding a little more parsley for taste and color.
